title: Turner syndrome: short stature and delayed puberty
desc: This station involves a focused history from the mother and a focused examination of a 13-year-old girl with short stature and absent puberty, then interpreting her growth chart, karyotype, blood tests, echocardiogram, renal ultrasound and audiology, explaining Turner syndrome and the management plan to the mother, and safety-netting.
stem: You are a GP. A mother has brought in her 13-year-old daughter because she is much shorter than her classmates and has not started puberty. A practice nurse is available to chaperone.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother and perform a focused examination of her daughter, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the growth chart and the results of the tests arranged after this visit: bone age, karyotype, blood tests, echocardiogram, renal ultrasound and audiology. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, explaining the diagnosis and plan to the mother, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are the mother of a 13-year-old girl. You are worried and want answers. Your daughter is with you; she is shy and answers briefly if spoken to directly, and agrees to be examined with you present. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine. Not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

Opening line: "She is much smaller than her friends and she hasn't started puberty."

History (give only when asked):

  • Growth: she has been the shortest in her class since primary school and seems to grow slowly. At her 4-year check the GP said she was below the bottom line on the chart, and she has stayed below it. She wears clothes made for much younger girls.
  • Puberty: no breast development and no periods. A little fine pubic hair this year. Your own periods began at 12. You are 165 cm and her father is 178 cm. No family history of short stature, late puberty or early menopause.
  • Birth: born at term weighing 2.7 kg. Her hands and feet were puffy for the first few weeks.
  • Ears: many ear infections as a toddler. She now struggles to hear in noisy classrooms.
  • Heart: a doctor once mentioned a soft heart murmur and it was never followed up. No chest pain, fainting, palpitations or breathlessness.
  • Kidneys: one urinary infection at age 5, none since.
  • Other symptoms: mildly tired and always feels the cold. No diarrhoea, abdominal pain, vomiting or weight loss. No headaches or change in vision. Eats well.
  • Development and school: development was normal. She finds maths hard but does well in English. She feels left out and embarrassed about her size, and some girls tease her.
  • Medicines, allergies, immunisations: none, none, up to date.
  • Family and social: lives with both parents and a younger brother, aged 9. You and your partner are thinking about having another baby.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you hope she is just a late bloomer who will catch up. You are worried it is a serious hormone problem and about her confidence. You expect tests, and help for her to grow and start puberty.

Question to raise in Part 1: "Is she just a late bloomer?"

In Part 2 the examiner puts your other questions to the candidate. Ask "What does that mean?" if the candidate uses jargon.
guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. In Part 2 the examiner hands over the growth chart and results, asks the questions in order and puts the mother's questions to the candidate.

A high-performing candidate takes a focused history that calculates the mid-parental height and finds the neonatal lymphoedema, ear infections, murmur and urinary infection. They examine with consent and a chaperone, find the Turner features, stage puberty and check arm and leg blood pressure and femoral pulses. They interpret every result correctly, give the diagnosis sensitively and without blame, outline endocrinology-led growth hormone and oestrogen induction, cardiology surveillance, thyroid, hearing, fertility and psychosocial care, and give specific red flags for aortic dissection.

A borderline candidate suspects a chromosomal cause but misses the cardiac and renal findings, does not explain why 30 cells are counted, misreads the gonadotrophins or thyroid results, uses jargon, rushes the explanation, or leaves out fertility, psychosocial support or specific safety netting.
explain:
Recognition

Turner syndrome (45,X or a variant) should be considered in any girl with unexplained short stature or delayed or arrested puberty. Height below the mid-parental range, neonatal lymphoedema, recurrent otitis media, a webbed neck, low hairline, wide carrying angle and widely spaced nipples support the diagnosis. No breast development by 13 meets the RCH referral criterion for delayed puberty. The RCH pre-referral work-up includes a karyotype in a girl with short stature, and thyroid function, coeliac serology, FSH, LH, oestradiol and a bone age X-ray (which shows how much growth remains) for delayed puberty. Constitutional delay is a diagnosis of exclusion: it does not explain dysmorphic features, a falling height velocity well below the mid-parental target, or raised gonadotrophins.

Interpreting the results

Her height has stayed below the 3rd centile with a slowing velocity and no growth spurt, far below her mid-parental height. A delayed bone age with open growth plates shows that growth remains, but bone age is also delayed in constitutional delay and hypothyroidism, so it does not make the diagnosis. A karyotype counting at least 30 cells detects low-level mosaicism (about 10% with 95% confidence). Y chromosome material carries a risk of gonadoblastoma: a marker chromosome needs further analysis (such as FISH) to find its origin, and a 45,X girl with signs of virilisation is screened for Y material by PCR or another molecular method. Her karyotype shows no marker and she has no clitoromegaly, so no further testing is needed. Raised LH and FSH with low oestradiol show ovarian insufficiency (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism); low gonadotrophins would instead point to a pituitary or hypothalamic cause or constitutional delay. A raised TSH with normal free T4 and positive anti-TPO is autoimmune thyroiditis, common in Turner syndrome. A negative tTG-IgA is only reassuring when total IgA is normal. Echocardiography (with cardiac MRI per cardiology) looks for bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation and aortic dilatation, which carry a lifelong risk of dissection. Renal ultrasound looks for a horseshoe kidney, and audiology for conductive and later sensorineural hearing loss.

Management

Paediatric endocrinology leads growth hormone treatment and oestrogen puberty induction. Induction is started on time (about 11 to 12 years), with low-dose oestradiol increased gradually, and it supports breast and uterine development and bone health. Thyroxine is decided by endocrinology. Fertility counselling covers premature ovarian insufficiency, donor oocytes and fertility preservation, and any pregnancy needs prior cardiac assessment. Care is lifelong, with cardiac, thyroid, coeliac, hearing, bone, metabolic and psychosocial follow-up and a planned transition to adult services.

Communication and safety netting

Give the news in private, in plain language, and say it is not the parents' fault. Allow time for emotion, and offer written information and support groups. Chest or tearing back pain, sudden breathlessness, palpitations or fainting need emergency review (aortic dissection). A horseshoe kidney raises the risk of urinary infection and obstruction, so fever with flank pain or burning urine needs a prompt urine test. Excessive thirst or passing a lot of urine needs a glucose check, as diabetes is more common in Turner syndrome.
points: Consider Turner syndrome in any girl with unexplained short stature or delayed puberty; compare height with the mid-parental height.
A karyotype should count at least 30 cells to detect mosaicism; look for Y material (FISH or PCR) when a marker chromosome is found or a 45,X girl shows virilisation.
Raised LH and FSH with low oestradiol indicate ovarian insufficiency; low gonadotrophins point elsewhere.
Screen for bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation and aortic dilatation, and for a horseshoe kidney; chest or tearing back pain needs emergency review.
Screen for thyroid disease, coeliac disease and hearing loss, and continue this lifelong.
Growth hormone and oestrogen induction are led by paediatric endocrinology; oestrogen is started at about 11 to 12 years and increased gradually.
refs: Gravholt CH, Andersen NH, Christin-Maitre S, et al. Clinical practice guidelines for the care of girls and women with Turner syndrome: proceedings from the 2023 Aarhus International Turner Syndrome Meeting. Eur J Endocrinol. 2024;190(6):G53-G151.
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne (RCH). Primary Care Liaison pre-referral guidelines: Short stature; Delayed puberty.

check.x: Professionalism
Handwashes, introduces self, confirms the identity of the mother and daughter, and explains the purpose of the consultation.
Uses sensitive, jargon-free language, acknowledges the mother's worry and includes the daughter in the conversation.
Asks consent for the examination, offers a chaperone and keeps the daughter covered during breast and pubertal staging.
History
Takes a growth and puberty history:

kids.x: Growth: shortest in class, below the bottom centile line since age 4, slow growth.
Puberty: no breast development or periods at 13, a little pubic hair; mother's menarche at 12.
Calculates the mid-parental height: (mother 165 cm plus father 178 cm minus 13) divided by 2 = 165 cm, and notes she is far below it.
Family history of short stature, late puberty or early menopause (none).

check.x: Asks about features associated with Turner syndrome:

kids.x: Puffy hands and feet as a newborn (lymphoedema) and low birth weight.
The heart murmur that was never followed up, and cardiac symptoms.

check.x: Screens for other causes: thyroid symptoms (tiredness, feeling the cold), coeliac symptoms, chronic illness and nutrition, headaches or visual change.
Asks about development and school (maths difficulty), mood and the social impact, medicines, allergies and immunisations.
Explores the mother's ideas, concerns and expectations, including the "late bloomer" idea.
Examination
Measures height and weight to plot on a growth chart, and notes proportionate short stature.

Looks for Turner features: webbed neck, low posterior hairline, low-set ears, high-arched palate, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, wide carrying angle, short fourth metacarpals, multiple naevi.
Stages puberty with consent and a chaperone: breast Tanner stage 1, pubic hair Tanner stage 2.
Examines the cardiovascular system for coarctation and a bicuspid aortic valve: blood pressure in the arm and leg, radial and femoral pulses for radio-femoral delay, and auscultation.
Examines the ears (otoscopy and a hearing check), the thyroid, and the spine for scoliosis.
Interpretation

Growth chart and bone age: height below the 3rd centile since age 4, slowing to 4 cm/year with no growth spurt, far below the mid-parental target; bone age delayed (11 years) with open growth plates, so growth remains.

Karyotype: 45,X in all 30 cells confirms Turner syndrome. Explains that counting at least 30 cells detects low-level mosaicism, and that Y chromosome material (which carries a risk of gonadoblastoma) is looked for with FISH or PCR only if a marker chromosome is seen or she shows signs of virilisation; neither applies here.
FSH 58 and LH 24 IU/L with oestradiol under 40 pmol/L show hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (primary ovarian insufficiency), so puberty will not start on its own.

TSH 7.8 mIU/L with a normal free T4 and positive anti-TPO is autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis with subclinical hypothyroidism, which may contribute to her tiredness and cold intolerance. Coeliac screen negative with a normal total IgA, so the screen is valid.
Echocardiogram: bicuspid aortic valve with no coarctation and a normal aortic size, which still needs lifelong cardiology surveillance because of the risk of aortic dilatation and dissection.
Renal ultrasound: horseshoe kidney without hydronephrosis, with a higher risk of urinary infection and obstruction. Audiology: mild bilateral conductive hearing loss needing ENT review.

States the diagnosis is Turner syndrome with primary ovarian insufficiency, and explains why other causes do not fit: constitutional delay (dysmorphic features, high FSH and LH, no family history), hypothyroidism or coeliac disease alone, and growth hormone deficiency or a pituitary problem (which give low, not high, gonadotrophins).
Management
Explains the diagnosis sensitively and checks understanding:

kids.x: A chromosomal condition in which all or some cells are missing one X chromosome.
A random event, not caused by anything the parents did; the chance of it happening in another pregnancy is very low.
Intelligence is usually normal, though maths and spatial tasks can be harder.
Pauses for emotion and offers time, written information and a second appointment.

check.x: Refers promptly to paediatric endocrinology to lead growth and puberty treatment, with dosing set by endocrinology:

kids.x: Growth hormone: benefit is greatest when started early, but it can still be considered at 13 while the growth plates are open. She will still be shorter than most women.

Oestrogen puberty induction: low-dose, usually transdermal oestradiol, started at about 11 to 12 years (so now) and increased gradually over 2 to 3 years, with a progestogen added later. It brings breast and uterine development, periods and bone protection.

check.x: Refers to paediatric cardiology for the bicuspid aortic valve: aortic surveillance (cardiac MRI when appropriate), blood pressure checks, and cardiology review before any future pregnancy.
Arranges repeat TSH and free T4 with endocrinology to decide on thyroxine, and ENT and audiology review for the hearing loss with classroom support.

Fertility: most women with Turner syndrome have ovarian insufficiency; pregnancy may be possible with donor eggs, and specialist fertility counselling will be offered when the family is ready; any pregnancy needs cardiac assessment first.

Arranges psychosocial and learning support, offers Turner syndrome support groups, and plans lifelong follow-up (thyroid, coeliac, blood pressure, hearing, bone and metabolic checks) with transition to an adult Turner clinic.
Safety netting
Tells the family to call 000 or go to the Emergency Department for chest pain or tearing back pain, sudden breathlessness, palpitations or fainting.

Advises prompt GP review for ear pain, discharge or worsening hearing; fever with flank pain or burning urine; persistent diarrhoea, abdominal pain or weight loss; excessive thirst or passing a lot of urine.
Arranges GP review within 2 weeks to check the referrals are booked and to support the family, with written information.

focus: Turner syndrome: short stature and delayed puberty in a girl

part2.lead: Three weeks later, the results of the tests you arranged are back. Here is her growth chart with her bone age, and the results.

handover.label: Growth chart and bone age
handover.result:
Growth chart (CDC girls, 2 to 20 years). Mid-parental height 165 cm (mother 165 cm, father 178 cm), about the 50th centile.

AgeHeightHeight centile
4 years92 cmbelow 3rd
8 years114 cmbelow 3rd
12 years134 cmbelow 3rd
13 years (today)138 cmwell below 3rd

Height velocity over the last year 4 cm/year, with no growth spurt. Weight 36 kg (about the 10th centile); BMI 18.9 kg/m2 (about the 50th centile).

Bone age (X-ray of the left hand and wrist, Greulich and Pyle): bone age 11 years at a chronological age of 13 years. Growth plates open. Short fourth metacarpal. No Madelung deformity.
handover.model:
Height has been below the 3rd centile since age 4 and is now well below it at 138 cm; she grew 4 cm in the last year with no pubertal spurt, and she is far below her mid-parental height of 165 cm. Weight and BMI are relatively preserved, so this is not undernutrition. Bone age is 11 years, 2 years behind, with open growth plates and a short fourth metacarpal.

For her: persistent short stature far below her genetic target, with no spurt at 13, is pathological rather than a late bloomer. A delayed bone age also occurs in constitutional delay and hypothyroidism, so it does not make the diagnosis, but the short fourth metacarpal fits Turner syndrome.

What it changes: with open growth plates growth remains, so growth hormone can still be considered now; refer to paediatric endocrinology.

handover.label: Karyotype (peripheral blood)
handover.result:
Cytogenetics report. Specimen: peripheral blood (lithium heparin). Method: lymphocyte culture, G-banded chromosome analysis at about 550 band resolution.

ItemFinding
Cells counted30
Cells analysed5
Cells karyotyped2
Karyotype (ISCN)45,X

Result: one X chromosome and no second sex chromosome in all 30 cells counted. No second cell line, no structurally abnormal X chromosome, no marker chromosome and no Y chromosome seen.

Interpretation: non-mosaic 45,X karyotype, consistent with Turner syndrome (monosomy X). Low-level mosaicism, or mosaicism confined to other tissues, cannot be excluded by this analysis. Genetic counselling is recommended.
handover.model:
45,X in all 30 cells counted: a single X chromosome, with no second cell line, structurally abnormal X, marker chromosome or Y chromosome seen. Counting at least 30 cells excludes mosaicism of 10% or more with 95% confidence.

For her: this confirms Turner syndrome (non-mosaic monosomy X), which explains her short stature, absent puberty and features. Y chromosome material, which carries a risk of gonadoblastoma, is looked for with FISH or PCR only if a marker chromosome is seen or she is virilised; she has neither (no clitoromegaly). 45,X is a random event, not caused by anything the parents did, and the chance of it in another pregnancy is very low.

What it changes: referral to paediatric endocrinology and genetic counselling, and screening for the associated conditions (heart, kidneys, hearing, thyroid, coeliac disease).

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.result: Reference intervals for a pubertal girl of 13 years; prepubertal (Tanner stage 1) values in brackets.
handover.model:
FSH 58 and LH 24 IU/L are far above the range for her age, let alone a prepubertal girl, with a prepubertal oestradiol below 40 pmol/L: hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (primary ovarian insufficiency). TSH 7.8 mIU/L with a normal free T4 of 14 pmol/L and positive anti-TPO antibodies is autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis with subclinical hypothyroidism. tTG-IgA is negative with a normal total IgA, so the coeliac screen is valid and negative.

For her: the ovaries are not working, so puberty will not start on its own. High gonadotrophins are against constitutional delay, growth hormone deficiency or a pituitary or hypothalamic cause, which give low gonadotrophins. The thyroiditis may add to her tiredness and feeling the cold, but it does not explain the whole picture.

What it changes: oestrogen puberty induction, led by endocrinology, is due now; repeat TSH and free T4 to decide on thyroxine; thyroid and coeliac screening continue for life.

handover.label: Echocardiogram
handover.result:
Examination: transthoracic echocardiogram. Clinical details: 13-year-old girl, 45,X Turner syndrome, soft ejection systolic murmur. Height 138 cm, weight 36 kg, body surface area 1.17 m2.

  • Situs solitus, levocardia; normal connections.
  • Aortic valve: bicuspid, with fusion of the right and left coronary cusps. Peak velocity 1.7 m/s, mean gradient 6 mmHg: no stenosis. No regurgitation.
  • Aorta: sinuses of Valsalva 23 mm, sinotubular junction 19 mm, ascending aorta 21 mm: normal for body surface area (z-scores below +2). Left aortic arch with normal branching. No coarctation: descending aortic peak velocity 1.4 m/s with no diastolic run-off; normal abdominal aortic pulsatility.
  • Ventricles: left ventricle normal in size and wall thickness, ejection fraction 64%. Right ventricle normal in size and function.
  • Other: mitral, tricuspid and pulmonary valves normal. Atrial and ventricular septa intact; no patent ductus arteriosus. Pulmonary venous drainage appears normal. No pericardial effusion.

Conclusion: bicuspid aortic valve (right and left cusp fusion) with normal function; no coarctation; normal aortic dimensions; normal heart size and function. Cardiac MRI recommended to assess the aorta and pulmonary veins, with cardiology follow-up.
handover.model:
A bicuspid aortic valve (right and left cusps fused) that works normally, with no stenosis or regurgitation; a normal left arch with no coarctation (no gradient or diastolic run-off); aortic dimensions normal for her size; normal heart size and function.

For her: it explains the soft murmur at the right upper sternal edge and fits her equal arm and leg pressures and normal femoral pulses. A bicuspid valve in Turner syndrome carries a lifelong risk of aortic dilatation and dissection, even with a normal aorta now.

What it changes: paediatric cardiology for lifelong aortic surveillance, including cardiac MRI; keep her blood pressure normal; cardiology review before any future pregnancy; and red flags for dissection (chest or tearing back pain, sudden breathlessness, fainting).

handover.label: Renal ultrasound
handover.result:
Examination: ultrasound of the renal tract. Clinical details: Turner syndrome (45,X); one urinary infection at age 5.

  • Kidneys: the lower poles are joined across the midline, in front of the aorta, by an isthmus of renal tissue 11 mm thick: a horseshoe kidney. Both halves lie low and are malrotated, so lengths are approximate: right 8.5 cm, left 8.8 cm.
  • Normal cortical thickness and echogenicity; corticomedullary differentiation preserved; no scarring.
  • No hydronephrosis (renal pelvis 4 mm right, 5 mm left, anteroposterior); no stones; ureters not dilated.
  • Bladder: well filled, smooth wall; post-void residual 5 mL.

Conclusion: horseshoe kidney without hydronephrosis, scarring or stones. Normal bladder.
handover.model:
A horseshoe kidney (the lower poles joined across the midline) with healthy renal tissue, no hydronephrosis, scarring or stones, and a normal bladder that empties.

For her: a common structural finding in Turner syndrome. It causes no symptoms now but carries a higher risk of urinary infection, obstruction at the pelviureteric junction and stones.

What it changes: no treatment; test the urine promptly with fever, flank pain or burning urine, and check blood pressure and kidney function as part of her lifelong follow-up.

handover.label: Audiology
handover.result:
Audiology assessment. Otoscopy: right drum dull and retracted with scarring; left tympanosclerosis; no discharge.

TestRight earLeft ear
Tympanometrytype B (flat), normal canal volumetype As (reduced compliance), normal pressure
Air conduction, 0.5 to 4 kHz30 to 40 dB HL (average 34)25 to 30 dB HL (average 28)
Bone conduction5 to 10 dB HL5 to 10 dB HL
Air-bone gap20 to 35 dB15 to 25 dB

Conclusion: mild bilateral conductive hearing loss, slightly worse on the right, with a flat right tympanogram suggesting middle ear fluid. Bone conduction normal: no sensorineural loss. Recommend ENT review, preferential seating in class, and repeat audiology after ENT treatment and then regularly.
handover.model:
Mild bilateral conductive hearing loss (air conduction averaging 34 dB right and 28 dB left with normal bone conduction), slightly worse on the right, where a flat tympanogram suggests middle ear fluid; the left drum is stiff from tympanosclerosis. No sensorineural loss yet.

For her: it fits her many ear infections and her trouble hearing in a noisy classroom. Middle ear disease is common in girls with Turner syndrome, and a sensorineural loss often develops later.

What it changes: ENT review (the right middle ear fluid may need treatment), preferential seating and support at school, and hearing checks for life.

ask: What is the diagnosis, and what else did you need to consider for her short stature and absent puberty?
What is your management approach, and who will you involve?
The mother asks: "Did I cause this? Could our next baby have it? Will she grow, go through puberty and be able to have children?" How do you answer?
What safety netting and follow-up will you arrange?
